claims.text: A Pulumi package is the unit of versioning and distribution, and the components inside a package inherit the package's version.
Pulumi recommends structuring Git repositories for publishing packages per the strategies in this guide (one package per repository, cohesive components).
Following these repository-structuring practices improves the reliability, maintainability, and delivery speed of the packages an organization builds and consumes.
Pulumi packages come in two flavors (source-based and executable-based), and each is versioned and released differently.
A source-based plugin package is distributed as source code in a Git repository, and its version is the Git tag on that repository.

Publishing a source-based package to the Pulumi IDP Private Registry is a two-step flow (apply a semver Git tag, then run `pulumi package publish`), typically performed by a CI/CD pipeline that runs on tag.
The first step of publishing a source-based package to the Private Registry is applying a semver Git tag (e.g., `v1.2.3`) to the repository.
`pulumi package publish` sends the package metadata to Pulumi Cloud and places the package in the Private Registry.
The `pulumi package publish` step often runs automated tests before publishing.
A CLI command reference page exists at /docs/iac/cli/commands/pulumi_package_publish/ for `pulumi package publish`.
Semver-tagged releases are only required for publishing to the Private Registry.
Source-based packages referenced directly from a `Pulumi.yaml` file can use any Git ref (tag, branch, or commit), regardless of whether it is a valid semantic version.

An executable-based plugin package is distributed as a pre-built plugin binary, typically alongside per-language SDKs published to package feeds (npm, PyPI, NuGet, Maven, the Go module proxy, or private equivalents).
The version of an executable-based package is the version embedded in the published binary and SDKs.
Pulumi Cloud customers can additionally publish an executable-based package to the Private Registry via `pulumi package publish`.
Executable-based package releases are produced by a CI/CD pipeline that builds the plugin, generates the SDKs, and pushes everything to the relevant feeds.

Link targets exist: packaging-components page anchors #source-based-plugin-packages and #executable-based-plugin-packages, the Private Registry concept page, and the packages/components concept pages.
In both cases (source-based and executable-based), the released artifact is a single, semantically-versioned Pulumi package.
A repository should contain exactly one Pulumi package, regardless of package type.
A repository containing multiple packages either has to release them in lockstep or invent per-package release tooling that fights the way Pulumi naturally consumes packages.
A 1:1 repository-to-package mapping keeps git tags, release artifacts, and version history aligned.
Multiple components inside a single Pulumi package are fine and expected, and the components ship together at the package's version.
Pulumi recommends: define exactly one package per repository, group a cohesive set of components in that package, and use multiple repositories (one per package) for distinct packages.

The Amazon EKS package in the Pulumi Registry (https://www.pulumi.com/registry/packages/eks/) bundles a managed Kubernetes cluster component along with supporting components needed to secure and operate it.
The components in the Pulumi EKS package are almost always used together and tend to evolve together.
A single `PulumiPlugin.yaml` at the repository root defines the package, with components living alongside it.
The example repository layout places `PulumiPlugin.yaml` at the repo root and components in a `components/` directory (EksCluster/, EksIam/).
Pulumi does not recommend using a single monorepo containing one giant package for all of an organization's components, because it forfeits meaningful semantic versioning.
Semantic versioning is how consumers know whether a given change is a bug fix, a new feature, or a breaking change.
When unrelated components share a package, every release of the package versions every component the same way, regardless of whether each component changed, which violates semver.
In the example sequence, an enhancement to ComponentA releases the package at v1.1.0 and a breaking change to ComponentB releases it at v2.0.0 (consistent with semver minor and major bumps).
Splitting unrelated components across separate, right-sized packages preserves the semver contract.
A Publishing packages guide exists at /docs/iac/guides/building-extending/packages/publishing-packages/.
